formation.title: The Loya Jirga at Kandahar
formation.text:
October 1747. The shrine of Sher-e-Surkh outside Kandahar is crowded with the chieftains of every Pashtun tribe. The Abdali, the Ghilji, the Yusufzai, the Mohmand; the Qizilbash captains, the Tajik notables, the Hindki merchants. Nadir Shah is dead, his army scattered, and the treasury of Persia has come home to Afghanistan in the saddlebags of the Abdali horsemen who once served him.

For nine days the jirga has argued. Some would have a council of equals, others a Shah. The mystic Sabir Shah Kabuli has settled it: he places a sheaf of wheat in the turban of the young Abdali commander and proclaims him Padshah. The Abdali henceforth shall be called Durrani, the Pearl of Pearls.

Now the choice falls to the new realm: shall it be the empire of the tribes, or the empire of the sword?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: By consensus of the jirga, we shall be the empire of the tribes.

modifiers.name: Loya Jirga of Kandahar
modifiers.text: The grand assembly of Pashtun chieftains has bound the tribes by oath. Manpower flows from every Abdali, Ghilji, and Tajik valley, and the standard of the new Shah is honoured from Herat to the Khyber.

options.text: By the standard of Ahmad Shah, we shall conquer from Mashhad to Delhi.

modifiers.name: Sword of Khorasan
modifiers.text: The Shah's army marches in the tradition of Nadir, descending from the Afghan highlands toward Persia and Hindustan. The Empire is built sabre by sabre, each campaign paid for in plunder.

advances.name: Pashtunwali Code
advances.text: The unwritten honour code of the Pashtuns, binding every tribesman to nanawatai, melmastia, badal, and nang. The Empire rules with the code, not against it.

event.title: The Pashtunwali
event.text: The unwritten code of the Pashtuns predates the Empire and outlives every dynasty. Nanawatai, the right of sanctuary; melmastia, the duty of hospitality; badal, the obligation of vengeance; nang, the demand of honour. No qazi enforces these laws, no Shah may abolish them, but every Pashtun, from the highest sardar to the lowest tribesman, lives by them. The Shah's wisdom is to rule with the code, not against it.

options.text: So shall it be among the Pashtuns.

advances.name: Bala Hissar Fortifications
advances.text: The mountain citadels of Kabul, Kandahar, Ghazni, and Herat command the passes. From their bastions the Shah holds the high country, even when the lowlands are lost.

event.title: The Bala Hissar of Kabul
event.text: On its shoulder of rock above Kabul, the Bala Hissar has stood since the days of the Hindu Shahis. Babur strengthened it, the Mughals garrisoned it, and now its bastions are rebuilt for the Durrani court. Sister citadels rise above Kandahar, Ghazni, and Herat. From these fortresses the Shah commands the high passes; an enemy who takes the lowlands has won nothing if the Bala Hissar remains.

options.text: The high citadels are the spine of the empire.

advances.name: Mountain Raiders
advances.text: The Pashtun tribesmen know every defile of the Hindu Kush. As light infantry they harry, ambush, and bleed any invader who climbs into their hills.

advances.name: Kandahari Horse Trade
advances.text: Kandahar is the great horse market of the crossroads, where Turkmen, Persian, and Indian buyers contend for the best Afghan stock.

advances.name: Rahdari Customs
advances.text: The rahdar officers post tolls at the Khyber, the Bolan, and Kabul gates, taxing every caravan that crosses between Hindustan, Persia, and Turan.

event.title: Customs of the Khyber
event.text: The great trans-Asian trade runs through our passes. Bukharan caravans bring fine horses, lapis, and slaves; Indian caravans bring spice, silk, and indigo; Persian merchants bring carpets and saffron. The rahdar officers stationed at the Khyber, the Bolan, and the Kabul gates report a swelling tide of traffic. The question is how heavily to tax it.

options.text: Tax every load. The treasury must be filled.

modifiers.name: Rahdari Tribute
modifiers.text: Every caravan over the Khyber and the Bolan pays toll in coin. The royal treasury grows on the back of the great trade between Persia, Turan, and Hindustan.

options.text: Keep the dues light. The trade itself enriches the empire.

modifiers.name: Open Passes
modifiers.text: Caravans move freely along the imperial roads, paying only modest dues. Bukharan and Indian merchants flock to the Afghan markets, and the bazaars of Kabul and Peshawar swell.

advances.name: Sufi Shrine Networks
advances.text: Naqshbandi and Qadiri orders bind tribe and crown through the khanaqahs and dargahs that dot the empire's roads.

advances.name: Hindki Merchant Communities
advances.text: The Hindu and Sikh trading families of Kabul, Peshawar, and Multan are kept under royal protection. Their networks reach to Bukhara, Lhasa, and Banaras.

advances.name: Khorasan Revival
advances.text: Persian poetry, Indo-Persian historiography, and Dari court letters flourish in the Durrani diwan. The Empire is heir to Khorasan as well as to Pashtunkhwa.

advances.name: Jirga Councils
advances.text: Tribal assemblies decide local matters by consensus. The Shah governs by council, not decree, and the Empire holds together because every chief feels heard.

advances.name: Hotaki Revival
advances.text: The memory of Mirwais Hotak's revolt against the Safavids steels Afghan arms. The Pashtuns once took Isfahan; they may do so again.

advances.name: Sistan Qanats
advances.text: Karez and qanat irrigation revives the Helmand basin and the wastes of Sistan. The empire's granaries fill where for centuries only nomads grazed.

advances.name: Naqshbandi-Mujaddidi Tariqa
advances.text: The renewed Sufi order of Sirhindi spreads through the empire. Its shaykhs preach a disciplined Sunni orthodoxy and bind the tribes to a single confessional cause.

event.title: Light of the Mujaddidi
event.text: The Naqshbandi-Mujaddidi tariqa, renewed by Shah Waliullah of Delhi and his Afghan disciples, has spread through the khanaqahs of Kabul, Peshawar, and Kandahar. Its shaykhs preach a sober Sunni orthodoxy and a discipline of the heart. Their writings circulate from the Volga to the Deccan. How shall the empire receive them?

options.text: Adopt their orthodoxy as the empire's confessional standard.

modifiers.name: Naqshbandi Unity
modifiers.text: The Mujaddidi shaykhs preach a renewed orthodoxy from the khanaqahs of Kabul and Peshawar. Sufi guidance binds tribesman, peasant, and townsman to a single confessional cause.

options.text: Embrace their wide humanism; many faiths share the realm.

modifiers.name: Cosmopolitan Tariqa
modifiers.text: The Sufi orders teach a wide tolerance, embracing Hindki traders, Qizilbash neighbours, and Sikh subjects. The mosque, the temple, and the gurdwara are all kept under the Shah's peace.

advances.name: Jezail Rifle Tradition
advances.text: Khyber gunsmiths produce the long-barrel matchlock, accurate to ranges no European musket can match. Pashtun marksmen dominate the broken country.

advances.name: Indo-Persian Court
advances.text: The Durrani diwan blends Persianate administration with Hindustani court forms. Munshis, mirzas, and pandits all serve the Shah.

advances.name: Council of Sardars
advances.text: The hereditary chiefs of the nine great Durrani tribes form the Shah's permanent council, raising levies and arbitrating between the clans.

advances.name: Abdali Heritage
advances.text: Sabir Shah's blessing renamed the Abdali the Durrani: the Pearl of Pearls. The dynasty bears the prestige of that founding.

advances.name: Loya Jirga Tradition
advances.text: The grand assembly of all Pashtun tribes is the constitutional foundation of the Empire. Each new Shah is acclaimed by it; each great war is sanctioned by it.

advances.name: Ghulam Khana
advances.text: The royal household guard, drawn from Pashtun, Tajik, and Qizilbash veterans. Mailed lancers loyal only to the Shah.

advances.name: Zamburak Corps
advances.text: Camel-mounted swivel guns, fast across desert and steppe. At Panipat two thousand zamburakis broke the Maratha line.

advances.name: Panipat Doctrine
advances.text: The Durrani way of war: heavy mailed cavalry on the wings, jezailchis in skirmish, zamburaks in mobile reserve. A doctrine forged in the great Indian campaigns.

event.title: The Third Battle of Panipat
event.text: 14 January 1761. On the dust plain north of Delhi, the Shah's mailed cavalry, his Rohilla allies, and two thousand swivel-mounted shutarnal camel guns face the host of the Maratha Confederacy. By dusk, sixty thousand of the enemy lie dead. Sadashivrao Bhau is killed; the Peshwa's heir is killed; the Maratha advance to the Indus is broken for a generation. The Shah holds the field, but his Afghan soldiers, unpaid for two years, are mutinous and longing for the cool of Kandahar.

options.text: Press the advantage; let the Hindustani princes know who rules the north.

modifiers.name: After Panipat
modifiers.text: The Marathas are broken on the field of Panipat. The Shah orders the campaign continued before the Hindustani princes can rally.

options.text: Return to Kandahar with the loot; rule what we have already won.

modifiers.name: Tribute of Panipat
modifiers.text: The army returns to Kandahar with the Koh-i-Noor and a year of plunder. The Empire turns to administration, integrating the conquered into the Shah's realm.

advances.name: Kandahar Treasury
advances.text: The royal mint and tribute repository at Kandahar receives the loot of Delhi, the customs of the Khyber, and the tribute of Sindh.

advances.name: Sadozai Succession
advances.text: The dynastic crisis after Timur Shah, when Sadozai princes contend at Kabul, Peshawar, and Herat. The way the empire navigates this crisis shapes its century.

event.title: After the Shah
event.text: Ahmad Shah is dead, and Timur Shah after him. The sons of the dynasty contend at Kabul, Peshawar, and Kandahar; the sardars of the Barakzai and the Popalzai weigh which prince to back. The Sikhs are stirring in Punjab, the Persians press at Mashhad, and the Empire's edges are fraying. The choice is whether to rule by crown or by council.

options.text: Crush the sardars; let the throne dictate to the tribes.

modifiers.name: Sadozai Crown
modifiers.text: The succession is settled by force of arms. The Sadozai house centralizes the realm, breaking rebellious sardars and asserting the Shah's writ from Herat to Lahore.

options.text: Govern through the sardars; the empire is their federation, not the king's.

modifiers.name: Council of Sardars
modifiers.text: The succession is settled by consensus. The tribal chiefs are confirmed in their lands and levies, and the Empire endures as a federation of Pashtun lords loyal to a first-among-equals.

advances.name: Frontier Defense
advances.text: The long retreat from Punjab and Sindh teaches the empire to fight on the defensive. Every gorge of the Hindu Kush becomes a fortress.

advances.name: Durrani Modernization
advances.text: Tentative reforms under the late Sadozai and early Barakzai shahs: the printing press at Kabul, the artillery school, the survey of the realm.

advances.name: Lashkar Reform
advances.text: The tribal levy is reorganized for modern war, with permanent regiments drawn from the Pashtun valleys and standardized arms.

destiny.name: The Long Road of the Empire
destiny.text: The Loya Jirga has crowned a Shah; now the empire must choose its long road. Either inward toward Khorasan, or outward toward Hindustan.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: The Long Road of the Empire
event.text: The Shah sits in council at the Bala Hissar. The Loya Jirga has spoken; the standard is raised; the treasury is full. But the question is what kind of empire this shall be: an empire of Khorasan, looking inward to its mountain plateau and the Persian-speaking world, or an empire of Hindustan, looking outward to the wealth of the Indus and the Yamuna. The sardars argue, the qazis quote, the Hindki merchants weigh their ledgers. The road must be chosen.

options.text: The road shall be ours to walk.

destiny.name: Khorasan Restored
destiny.text: Reclaim the Persianate heartland. Take Mashhad and Nishapur and stabilize the realm; the empire's centre of gravity returns to where Khorasan, Sistan, and the Hindu Kush meet.

conditions.text: Loya Jirga path chosen
Own Mašhad, or a subject owns it
Own Nīshāpūr, or a subject owns it
Stability at least 25

event.title: Khorasan Returns to the Pearl
event.text: Mashhad and Nishapur are ours. The shrine of the Imam Reza is again under Sunni administration; the bazaars of Nishapur send their carpets, saffron, and turquoise to Kandahar. The Persian-speaking notables of Khorasan ride to the Shah's diwan, and the Khorasani culture which has always been the empire's twin language now becomes its administrative spine. The wastes of the Helmand basin and the orchards of Herat are ours by right and by history.

options.text: Khorasan is the soul of the empire.

destiny.name: Pearls of the Federation
destiny.text: Develop the Khorasani heartland into the empire's economic core. Take Merv and Bukhara, raise Herat, the pearl of Khorasan, to half again its size, and fill the treasury. The qanat circuit is the empire's spine.

conditions.text: Own Merv, or a subject owns it
Own Bukhara, or a subject owns it
Owns Herat and its development is at least 34
Gold at least 2000

event.title: The Qanat Circuit
event.text: Merv and Bukhara are taken. The empire's mirabs survey the qanat lines from Sistan to Khwarezm; the Hindki bankers underwrite a hundred new caravan stages; the Hazara peasants dig new karez under royal warrant. There is more to do than there are hands. The Shah's diwan must decide: shall the qanat circuit be expanded by corvee, the labor of the realm pressed into imperial works? Or shall the trade itself fund the works, the caravans bringing the silver that pays the diggers?

options.text: Press the corvee. The qanat is built by the realm itself.

modifiers.name: Qanat Corvee
modifiers.text: The empire's labor is pressed into the qanat works. New shafts run from Sistan to Khwarezm; villages thrive at the heads of new channels. The realm grows by water and stone.

options.text: Tax the caravans. The trade itself shall fund the works.

modifiers.name: Caravan Circuit
modifiers.text: The trade pays for itself. Bukharan, Indian, and Persian caravans flow through the Khorasani circuit; Kabul, Herat, and Kandahar swell with new merchants and bazaaris. The diwan dispatches its diplomats wide.

destiny.name: Sunni Imamate of Khorasan
destiny.text: Stand as the Sunni Imamate of Khorasan: heir to the Samanids, rival to the Safavid throne, and patron of the qanat-monastery network. Take Samarkand and Isfahan, build Kandahar, the city Ahmad Shah laid out anew, to twice its size, and unlock the Khorasani Qanat Network as your imperial irrigation work.

conditions.text: Own Samarkand, or a subject owns it
Own Esfahân, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 3000
Owns Kandahar and its development is at least 19

event.title: Imam of the Sunna
event.text: Samarkand and Isfahan are taken. The empire stretches from the Aral steppe to the Persian Gulf, and the Shah is now the unrivalled patron of Sunni Khorasan, with the shrine of Imam Reza, the tomb of Tamerlane, and the Friday mosque of Isfahan all in his hand. From Naqshbandi shaykhs to Hindki bankers, every voice of the empire asks the same question: shall the Shah be the Imam of the Sunna, defender of the orthodox faith and rival to the Safavids' Shia mantle? Or shall he keep the Durrani Horizon, the wide tolerance of the Persianate ecumene?

options.text: I am Imam of the Sunna; the orthodox creed is my standard.

modifiers.name: Imam of the Sunna
modifiers.text: The Shah is acclaimed Imam of the Sunna. The shrines of Imam Reza, of Tamerlane, of Naqshband all are under his patronage; his armies fight under the green standard of orthodoxy and the empire is the rival of every Shia throne.

effects.name: Damage Done versus Heathens in Battle

options.text: The Durrani Horizon: many faiths under one Persianate roof.

modifiers.name: The Durrani Horizon
modifiers.text: The empire is the wide tolerant Persianate ecumene of poets, mystics, traders, and scholars. The Hindki banker, the Naqshbandi shaykh, the Qizilbash captain, the Hazara mirab all walk under one imperial sky.

destiny.name: March on the Indus
destiny.text: Continue Ahmad Shah's invasions. Take Lahore and Multan, and hold the crossing of the Indus at Attock. The wealth and population of Hindustan are within the Shah's reach.

conditions.text: Sword of Khorasan path chosen
Own Lahore, or a subject owns it
Own Multan, or a subject owns it
Own Attock, or a subject owns it

event.title: March on the Indus
event.text: Lahore and Multan have fallen. The Shah's army stands on the Indus and looks east, where the Mughal pretender holds Delhi only by sufferance, the Marathas raid the Doab, the Sikhs harry the Punjab, and the Jats hold the Yamuna. None of these powers can field what we have fielded. The Hindustani plain lies open. The campaign continues.

options.text: Onward to Delhi.

destiny.name: The Loot of Delhi
destiny.text: Sack Delhi and the Doab. Take Delhi, Agra, and Sirhind; bring back the loot of the Mughal capital. The Peacock Throne is yours by right of conquest.

conditions.text: Own Delhi, or a subject owns it
Own Agra, or a subject owns it
Own Sirhind, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 2000

event.title: The Loot of Delhi
event.text: Delhi has fallen, and Agra, and Sirhind. The Mughal Emperor sits as our pensioner; the Peacock Throne is broken up and shipped to Kandahar; the Koh-i-Noor is in the saddlebag of the Shah. Forty crores in tribute have been promised. Yet the Doab is restless and the Maratha confederacy has not yet been broken. Two voices contend in the diwan: chastise the rebel princes by the sword, or rule them through Hindustani administrators in Mughal forms?

options.text: Chastise them. The sword is the only language the princes know.

modifiers.name: Chastise the Doab
modifiers.text: The princes of the Doab are taught by the sword. The empire's heavy infantry, jezailchi skirmishers, and zamburak corps drill for the next campaign; rebel forts fall faster than they can be raised.

options.text: Rule through the Yamuna diwan; let the munshis administer.

modifiers.name: The Yamuna Diwan
modifiers.text: Hindustani munshis and Mughal-trained administrators staff the new imperial diwan on the Yamuna. The empire integrates its conquests through paper, register, and firman.

destiny.name: Pearl of Pearls Crowned
destiny.text: Make the Indus your river and Kabul your imperial seat. Hold Srinagar, Thatta, and Peshawar; build Kabul to twice its size; let the Bala Hissar of Kabul rise as the Imperial Diwan, the Mughal mantle taken in earnest.

conditions.text: Own Srinagar, or a subject owns it
Own Thatta, or a subject owns it
Own Peshawar, or a subject owns it
Owns Kabul and its development is at least 40
Prestige at least 75

event.title: Padshah-e Hind
event.text: Srinagar of Kashmir, Thatta of Sindh, Peshawar of the Khyber, and Kabul grown to twice the town it was. The Shah is acclaimed Padshah-e Hind, master of all the lands from the Oxus to the Yamuna. The Bala Hissar of Kabul rises as a new imperial seat, modelled on the Red Fort, with diwans for the Pashtun nobles, the Hindustani munshis, the Hindki bankers, and the Persian poets. Now the question: rule as the Mughal mantle taken whole, or rule from Kabul as the imperial Durrani capital, distinct from the Mughal past?

options.text: I take the Mughal mantle. I am Padshah-e Hind.

modifiers.name: Padshah-e Hind
modifiers.text: The Shah takes the Mughal mantle in earnest. From the Oxus to the Yamuna, the empire's standard is the Padshah-e Hind, and the heavy Pashtun cavalry rides under a new imperial sun.

options.text: Kabul is the imperial seat. The Durrani realm is its own.

modifiers.name: The Kabul Diwan
modifiers.text: Kabul is the seat of the empire, not Delhi. The Bala Hissar rises as the imperial diwan, with hall of audience, garden of audience, and library; ambassadors of every land attend the Shah in the high citadel.

units.name: Pashtun Lashkar
units.text: Tribal warband levied through the loya jirga. Each man brings his own jezail or tulwar; collectively they are the spine of the Empire's army and a terror in their home mountains.

units.name: Jezailchi
units.text: Long-barrel matchlock skirmisher from the Khyber gunsmith villages. Famous for picking off officers at ranges no European musket can reach, and for vanishing back into the rocks when charged.

units.name: Ghulam Khana
units.text: Royal household heavy cavalry. Mailed lancers drawn from Pashtun, Tajik, and Qizilbash veterans, sworn personally to the Shah.

units.name: Zamburak
units.text: A swivel gun mounted on a kneeling camel. Fast across desert and stony ground, devastating at the close range that broke the Marathas at Panipat.

units.name: Zamburak Levy
units.text: Tribal swivel-gunners raised through the soldiers and tribesmen of the Empire. Cheaper than the regular zamburak corps, but fights with the same fearsome sting.

units.name: Ghazi
units.text: Pashtun frontier warriors of the Hotaki revival, called to jihad against the Safavids and the Marathas. Heavy shock infantry that fights with religious fervor in the broken country.

units.name: Kohistani Light Infantry
units.text: Modernized mountain infantry of the late Sadozai and Barakzai era. Drilled in European fashion but still at home in the gorges of the Hindu Kush.

buildings.name: Bala Hissar
buildings.text: Mountain citadel commanding a city and its passes. The Bala Hissar of Kabul, the Arg of Kandahar, and the Citadel of Herat all follow this pattern.

buildings.name: Rahdari Post
buildings.text: Customs station on the imperial caravan roads. Rahdar officers register caravans, levy tolls, and dispatch mounted escorts.

buildings.name: Jezail Workshop
buildings.text: Khyber gunsmith house producing the long-barrel matchlock. The barrels are forged of pattern-welded iron and fitted with delicately curved stocks.

buildings.name: Royal Treasury
buildings.text: The royal mint and tribute repository at Kandahar. Built to hold the Koh-i-Noor and the loot of Delhi, it became the financial spine of the Empire.

buildings.name: Kandahari Horse Market
buildings.text: The great regional horse fair where Turkmen, Persian, and Indian buyers contend for the best Afghan stock. The treasury thrives on its tolls.

buildings.name: Sufi Khanaqah
buildings.text: Naqshbandi or Qadiri lodge combining shrine, seminary, and hostel for travelling dervishes. The shaykhs bind tribesmen and townsmen alike to the Empire's confessional life.

buildings.name: Hindki Quarter
buildings.text: Hindu and Sikh trading enclave under royal firman. Their family networks reach Bukhara, Lhasa, and Banaras, channeling trade through the Empire's bazaars.

buildings.name: Kabul Lithographic Press
buildings.text: The first Afghan printing press, established under Barakzai patronage at Kabul. Dari and Pashto books spread literacy and lay the foundation of a modern Afghan public.

buildings.name: Khorasani Qanat Network
buildings.text: An imperial irrigation work uniting the karez and qanat lines from Sistan to Khwarezm. Mirabs of the diwan survey new shafts every season; the orchards of Herat, Mashhad, and Bukhara feed an empire.

buildings.name: Imperial Diwan of Kabul
buildings.text: The Bala Hissar of Kabul rebuilt as the imperial seat, modelled on the Red Fort of Delhi. Pashtun sardars, Hindustani munshis, Hindki bankers, and Persian poets all attend the Shah in his hall of audience.

list.name: Loya Jirga
list.text: The grand assembly of Pashtun chieftains. In October 1747, after the assassination of Nader Shah, nine days of debate at the shrine of Sher-i Surkh in Kandahar elected Ahmad Shah Abdali (later Durrani) as padshah-i durr-i-durran (pearl of pearls). Every Sadozai succession after his death was confirmed at a similar jirga, and the Abdali, Ghilji, Tajik and Hazara khans expected to be heard. The institution constrained the Shah but bound every tribe by oath to the imperial standard; manpower flowed from valleys whose chiefs could not be coerced but could be honoured.

list.name: Diwan-i-A'la
list.text: The supreme chancery of the wazir, modelled on Safavid and Mughal high diwans. Shah Wali Khan Bamizai, wazir to Ahmad Shah from 1761, ran imperial finance, drafted firmans, and supervised the provincial subadars of Kashmir, Punjab, Sindh and Khorasan. Persian was its language, Indo-Persian munshis its clerks. The diwan was a counterweight to the Pashtun sardars whose loyalties were tribal first; when the chancery functioned, revenue flowed and the firmans were obeyed. When it failed (as it did during the post-1772 succession crises under Timur Shah's sons), the empire fragmented along the lines the diwan had been built to suppress.

list.name: Hindki Sarrafs
list.text: The Multani, Shikarpuri and Khatri banking houses that operated hundi credit networks from Astrakhan to Hyderabad. Hindu and Sikh sarrafs and arhatiyas held the imperial revenue contracts of Punjab, Sindh and the trans-Indus passes; their hundis financed Ahmad Shah's eight invasions of Hindustan, including the field army that won at Panipat in 1761. Maliki-minded ulama resented the depth of dhimmi participation in imperial finance and occasionally pressed for jizya enforcement. The empire ignored them: the zamburak gunners and qizilbash horse could not be paid in fatwas.

list.name: Naqshbandi-Mujaddidi Mashaikh
list.text: The Sufi tariqa founded by Imam Rabbani Sirhindi (d. 1624) and continued by Shah Waliullah of Delhi (d. 1762). Naqshbandi pirs of the Mujaddidi line crossed the Pashtun belt, blessing Ahmad Shah's invasions of Hindustan as defence of the umma against the Marathas and Sikhs and binding the rural tribes to the throne through their khanaqahs at Peshawar, Kabul, and Kandahar. The mashaikh gave the Sadozai a religious legitimacy independent of Mughal Delhi, but a clergy that could anathemise a wayward shah as easily as it had crowned him.

conditions.text: Sunnism religion
